name: Elk velvet antler

card.summary: A supplement made from the soft, growing antler of elk (wapiti), taken in capsules or sprays for recovery, joints and training, which can support a better physique.
card.note: Antler sprays can be flagged by sport anti-doping bodies because of possible IGF-1 and contamination.

quick.overview:
Elk velvet antler is the soft, hair-covered antler of elk (wapiti) harvested while it is still growing, then dried and sold as capsules, powders or sprays. It has a long history in traditional Chinese and Korean medicine and is marketed in the West for joint comfort, recovery and athletic performance, which is how people connect it to looking and training better.

Human trials have mostly tested it in rheumatoid arthritis and in athletes. A 2012 systematic review found seven randomised trials with no convincing benefit for any condition, though it saw some promise for osteoarthritis, and a 10-week study in rowers found no difference in strength, performance or hormones versus placebo.
quick.how: People take velvet antler as daily capsules or powders, or as sublingual sprays, usually for joint and recovery support alongside training. Some stack it with collagen or joint supplements. Trials ran from weeks to six months.
quick.risks: In studies, elk velvet antler was tolerated alongside standard arthritis treatment. The FDA has sent warning letters over disease claims for velvet antler, and sports bodies including MLB have warned about contamination; WADA noted antler sprays may contain IGF-1 that could cause a positive test. Lidocaine residues have been found in antler harvested with anaesthetic.

lead: Elk velvet antler is the soft, uncalcified antler of elk, called wapiti, covered in velvet and harvested during growth. Elk, red deer and sika deer are the main sources, and New Zealand is the largest producer [1]. In traditional Chinese medicine it is known as lurong and used mainly for yang deficiency [1].

In appearance and fitness circles it is promoted for joint health, recovery, strength and testosterone or growth-factor support, so that people can train more and build a better physique. Spray forms became widely discussed around 2013 for claimed IGF-1 content [1].

A 2012 systematic review of randomised trials found seven studies and concluded that claims for velvet antler are not based on rigorous human research, though osteoarthritis findings may have some promise [2].

angle.text: Users take elk velvet antler hoping for joint comfort and faster recovery so they can train harder. Trials in rowers did not show changes in strength or hormones, and studies in arthritis were mixed.

infobox: Elk (wapiti); also red deer, sika deer

paras: Velvet antler is the entire antler of Cervidae while still soft and covered in velvet. It is sold dried in slices or powder, boiled in soups, or processed into capsules, extracts and sprays [1]. Korean and Chinese traders divide the antler into sections with different supposed uses, such as child growth, joints and bones, and calcium for older people [1]. Russia produced an alcohol extract called Pantocrin from the 1930s to the 1980s [1].

Elk velvet antler is taken for joint comfort, recovery and athletic performance. A T Nation forum thread on deer antler velvet discusses it in connection with testosterone and cites the rower trial [10]. Sprays were promoted for injury recovery and performance, and endocrinologists reportedly consider the IGF-1 in sprays too small to have an effect [1].

Animal work includes studies of lifelong elk velvet antler feeding in rats, which examined growth, bone development and toxicity [6][7]; a topical study in diabetic rats on wound healing [8]; and a trial in dogs with osteoarthrosis [9]. A 2009 review of canine osteoarthritis therapies assessed treatments of several kinds [11].

The FDA has sent warning letters to firms claiming velvet antler treats or prevents disease and has said such claims would require drug approval; as of 2018, powders, extracts and sprays can be sold as supplements without disease claims and with the standard disclaimer [1]. WADA banned deer antler spray and lifted the ban in early 2013 while warning it may contain IGF-1, and Major League Baseball prohibited it in 2011 over potential contamination [1]. Alabama's attorney general ordered supplier S.W.A.T.S. to shut down in 2013 over deceptive claims [1]. Lidocaine residues have been measured in elk velvet antler [12].

A 2012 systematic review of RCTs of deer and elk velvet antler found seven trials: two in rheumatoid arthritis, one in osteoarthritis, one in sexual function and three in sport performance. Two reported some positive effects but neither was convincing and five found no effect [2].

A six-month triple-blind trial of 168 people with stage 2 to 3 rheumatoid arthritis found no significant differences between elk velvet antler and placebo on any measure [3], and an earlier phase II trial of 40 patients tested safety with arthritis medications [4].
In 46 male and female rowers taking 560 mg a day for 10 weeks of training, strength, VO2max and 2000 m times improved equally with antler and placebo, and hormone responses did not differ [5].

timeline.event: Russia produces the velvet antler extract Pantocrin [1].
MLB prohibits deer antler spray over contamination concerns [1].
Systematic review of velvet antler RCTs published [2].
WADA lifts its ban on antler spray; Alabama orders S.W.A.T.S. to shut down [1].

lore.intro: Velvet antler is discussed in lifting forums as a natural testosterone, IGF-1 or recovery aid.

claims.claim: Velvet antler raises testosterone and growth factors and builds muscle
claims.believers: Spray marketers and forum posters say it supplies IGF-1 and supports gains [10][1].
claims.experts: A trial in rowers found no change in hormone response or performance; endocrinologists reportedly say the IGF-1 content is too small to act [5][1].

claims.believers: Traditional use and marketing cite joint support [1].
claims.experts: A six-month trial in rheumatoid arthritis found no difference from placebo; the review saw some promise in osteoarthritis [3][2].
